questions.q: For classical unstructured search over N=8 items with one marked item, what are the worst-case and average-case query counts?
options: 8 worst case, 8 average case
2 worst case, 1 average case
8 worst case, 4.5 average case
4 worst case, 2 average case
questions.explain: Worst case requires checking all 8 items; average case follows the (N+1)/2 expectation formula, giving (8+1)/2 = 4.5.

questions.q: Using Chapter 4's verified N=8 Grover table, how many oracle calls achieve the highest success probability, and what is that probability?
options: 1 oracle call, 100% success probability
4 oracle calls, 94.53% success probability
2 oracle calls, 94.53% success probability
8 oracle calls, 100% success probability
questions.explain: The verified table shows probability rising to a peak of 0.9453 at 2 iterations (matching ⌊(π/4)√8⌋=2), then falling at 3 and 4 iterations.

questions.q: Why can't the '2 oracle calls vs 4.5 classical checks' comparison be directly read as a fair wall-clock comparison for a concrete search problem?
options: Because Grover's algorithm doesn't actually use an oracle
Because classical checks are always more expensive than oracle calls
Because oracle calls and classical checks always take exactly the same amount of time
Because each oracle call is itself a quantum circuit whose gate cost depends on how complex the 'is this the marked item?' check is, which can be far more expensive than one classical comparison
questions.explain: Query count and real-world cost are different things (Rule 2 of the benchmarking checklist) — the oracle's own implementation cost has to be accounted for before concluding a real speedup.

questions.q: Why does structured data (sorted arrays, hash tables) make Grover's algorithm irrelevant for many real-world 'search' problems?
options: Because Grover's algorithm cannot run on structured data at all, even in principle

Because classical algorithms exploiting that structure (binary search O(log N), hashing O(1)) already beat Grover's O(√N) outright, with no quantum hardware needed, and Grover's regime is specifically the unstructured case
Because sorted arrays make the marked item impossible to find
Because hash tables and quantum computers are mathematically incompatible
questions.explain: Grover's quadratic advantage only matters when there is no structure to exploit. The moment a problem has exploitable structure, classical approaches like binary search or hashing are already faster than even an idealized Grover's algorithm.

questions.q: Why would a real quantum device likely see a lower success rate than the idealized 94.53% computed for N=8, 2 iterations?
options: Because real quantum computers always outperform theoretical predictions
The 94.53% figure comes from a noiseless matrix simulation; real hardware has gate errors and decoherence that degrade the idealized probability
Because N=8 is too small a search space for Grover's algorithm to apply
Because 94.53% was computed incorrectly and the real value is always exactly 50%
questions.explain: Rule 5 of honest benchmarking requires stating the error model. The verified 94.53% assumes a perfect, noiseless circuit; real noisy hardware introduces errors that this idealized number does not account for.
